changes.after: A clock offset tells you how far local time is ahead of or behind UTC.

before:
Time.utc constructs a known UTC instant. getlocal(offset) returns a new Time representation with that offset; it does not change the original. strftime formats fields using directives such as %Y year, %m month, %d day and %H:%M time.

The shown Time.utc arguments are year, month, day, hour and minute, in that order: (2025, 1, 1, 0, 30) means 00:30 on January 1, 2025 in UTC. Seconds are omitted and default to zero here.

The -05:00 offset here is explicit and fixed. It does not model a region with daylight-saving transitions. Avoid current-clock assertions, and distinguish elapsed duration from calendar-day arithmetic. Ruby Time also has mutating conversions such as localtime; do not assume every time API is immutable.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
instant = Time.utc(2025, 1, 1, 0, 30)
local = instant.getlocal("-05:00")
puts instant.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
puts local.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")

```

Expected output or behavior: 2025-01-01 00:30
2024-12-31 19:30. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Make a local view of the same instant without changing the UTC value.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
instant = Time.utc(2025, 1, 1, 0, 30)
local = instant.getlocal("-05:00")
puts instant.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
puts local.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
```
The output is `2025-01-01 00:30`, then `2024-12-31 19:30`. Half past midnight in UTC shows as half past seven the previous evening at this offset.
